en: *The Treatise on the Precious Conduct for Kings*, One Scroll, translated by Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master from India during the Chen Dynasty.
Chapter One: On Peaceful Bliss and Liberation. Chapter One: On Peaceful Bliss and Liberation.
Liberated from all obscurations, adorned with perfect virtues, I pay homage to the Honored One of All-Knowledge, the true and virtuous friend of sentient beings.
The True Dharma is definitively good; for those who love the Dharma, he is the Great King.
I shall now speak of the Dharma, which flows into those who are vessels for the Dharma.
First I will explain the Dharma that is the cause of happiness; later I will analyze the Dharma of liberation.
Thus, sentient beings first attain peace and happiness, and subsequently achieve liberation.
The requisites of virtue are called "happiness," and liberation is said to be the exhaustion of delusions;
briefly stated, the causes for these two are solely the two faculties of faith and wisdom.
Through faith one is able to uphold the Dharma, and through wisdom one understands it as it truly is.
Among the two, wisdom is supreme; first, one initiates practice by relying on faith.
One who, despite delusion, greed, hatred, and fear, is able not to destroy the Dharma—know that such a person possesses faith, a vessel for auspiciousness and happiness.
Having already mastered the thorough discernment of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind,
and constantly benefiting both oneself and others— such a person is said to be wise.
Killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and divisive talk,
Harsh abuse, improper speech, greed, hatred, and wrong views—these dharmas are called the ten unwholesome actions;
the opposite of these are the ten wholesome actions.
Abstinence from alcohol constitutes a pure livelihood; giving with a mind free from oppression and affliction,
One should make offerings to those worthy of veneration; this is the brief teaching on the Dharma.
If one practices only asceticism, wholesome dharmas will certainly not arise, for it is devoid of wisdom and compassion.
Unable to remove harm from others, yet providing rescue and benefit—this is what is clarified through generosity, morality, and cultivation: the great level path of the True Dharma.
If one abandons this to practice deviant paths, one will suffer self-inflicted pain and receive the punishment of an ox.
This wilderness of birth and death has neither food nor drink, nor the shade of trees;
one may be devoured by wolves as one travels through it for a vast duration.
Because of killing, one’s life is shortened; because of oppression and affliction, one invites much illness.
Through stealing, one suffers from lack of wealth; by encroaching on another’s territory, one incurs much resentment;
through lying, one meets with slander; through divisive speech, one is separated from loved ones;
through harsh words, one hears what is unpleasant; and through frivolous talk, one is held in hatred and jealousy by others.
Through greed one harms what is sought; through anger one suffers terror;
through wrong views one gives rise to perverse attachments; through drinking alcohol the mind becomes dull and disordered.
Because of not practicing giving, one is poor; because of a wrong livelihood, one encounters deception.
Lack of reverence leads to low birth; jealousy results in a lack of majesty and virtue.

Constant resentment over one’s own ugly form and stupidity due to failing to seek wisdom—this retribution is received within the human realm, though it was preceded by suffering in the evil destinies.
The karmic retributions for unwholesome dharmas such as killing are as previously described;
non-attachment and other such states, along with their corresponding actions, are called the causes of wholesome cultivation.
All forms of evil practice and suffering arise from false dharmas.
The peace and happiness of all good realms arise entirely from wholesome dharmas;
one should always avoid all evil and constantly practice all that is good.
Through the actions of body, speech, and mind, one should understand these two principles.
By one dharma one can be liberated from the four realms of existence, such as hell;
by the second dharma one can experience the wealth and joy of kings among men and gods.
Through meditative concentration, the Brahma-abodes, and emptiness, one attains the bliss of Brahmā and other such states.
Thus, the names of the causes of happiness and the fruits of happiness have been briefly explained.
Furthermore, the Dharma of liberation is subtle, profound, and difficult to perceive;
when ordinary people, who lack both ears and wisdom, hear of it, they give rise to fear and trepidation.
"I shall not exist in the future, nor do I exist in the present;
ordinary people fear when they contemplate this, but for the wise, fear is forever exhausted.
The view of self arises in the world, bound by attachment to the affairs of others."
The Buddha, having realized it through the supreme path, taught it to others out of compassion.
"I" and "mine"—these two are in truth both empty;
by seeing reality as it truly is, the two types of grasping no longer arise.
The grasping at a self arises from the aggregates; since this grasping at a self is empty of reality, if the seed is not real, how can the sprout and so forth be true?
If one sees that the aggregates are unreal, the view of a self will not arise.
Through the extinction of the view of self, the aggregates no longer arise.
Just as a person relying on a clear mirror can see the reflection of their own face—
a reflection that is merely visible and is in every respect unreal.
The view of self is likewise: it manifests in dependence upon the aggregates;
yet when examined according to reality, it is found not to exist, just like a reflection on the surface of a mirror.
Just as a person who does not hold up a mirror does not see the reflection of their own face, so too, without the aggregates, the self cannot be perceived.
Thus, when the aggregates are analyzed, the view of a self no longer exists.
Having heard this teaching, the Venerable Ānanda attained the pure Dharma-eye and has constantly taught this to others.
As long as the grasping at the aggregates persists, the view of self likewise remains constant;
because the view of self exists, karma and existence perpetually arise.
This wheel of birth and death revolves through three links, without beginning, middle, or end.
Just as a whirling firebrand arises through mutual dependence, so too do self, other, and both arise from one another.
Since they do not exist across the three times, when this is realized, the view of a self is extinguished; subsequently, the same applies to karma and its retribution.
Seeing cause and effect in this way— both their arising and their cessation—
one does not cling to the world as being truly existent or non-existent.
When fools hear this Dharma, they are able to exhaust all suffering.
Fear arises from ignorance regarding that which is not to be feared;
this does not exist in the state of nirvāṇa, so why do you give rise to fear?
Since it is as described—true emptiness—how could it cause you to be afraid?
Liberation is the absence of self and aggregates; if you were to accept this Dharma, you would abandon both the self and the aggregates—why then do you not rejoice?
Even non-existence is not Nirvana, let alone existence.
The exhaustion of the grasping at existence and non-existence—this the Buddha calls nirvana.
To speak briefly of wrong views, they consist in the denial of cause and effect;
this is now a lack of merit, the heaviest cause for rebirth in the evil realms.
To speak briefly of right view: it is the conviction that cause and effect exist;
it can fulfill one's merit and is the supreme cause for the happy realms.
Through wisdom, one attains the peace of both existence and non-existence, thereby transcending both merit and demerit.
Therefore, being free from the paths of good and evil, the Buddha calls it liberation.
If one perceives that birth has a cause, the wise person abandons clinging to non-existence;
by perceiving that cessation shares the same cause, they therefore abandon clinging to existence.
The two causes that arise simultaneously are not causes in the ultimate sense;
for as mere designations they lack a basis, and because their arising is not real.
That "this being, that exists" is like the relationship between long and short.
From this arising, that arises, just like a lamp and its light.
It is not the case that what was long first becomes short later, because such a nature does not exist;
and since light is not produced [independently], the lamp, too, is not substantially real.
When the arising of such cause and effect is seen as neither existent nor non-existent,
one has already gained faith in the reality of the world; because it arises from a distracted mind,
seeing its cessation as not false, one immediately realizes *tathatā*.
Therefore, one does not cling to existence, nor does one rely on dualistic liberation.
Form is seen from afar; if it were most distinct when near, why would a mirage, if it were real, not be seen when one is close?
If one is far from true wisdom, one perceives the world as existing;
yet upon realizing the truth, it is no longer seen. It is signless, like the mirage of a deer’s thirst.
Like the deer’s thirst which appears to be water, it is neither water nor a real substance.
Thus these aggregates resemble a person, yet they are neither a person nor a real entity.
To reckon the mirage as water and go there to drink it—
if one does not grasp at it as water, then such a person is free from delusion.
The world is like the thirst of a deer; if one clings to existence or non-existence as real, this is precisely ignorance, and due to such delusion there is no liberation.
Clinging to non-existence leads to the evil realms, while clinging to existence leads to the good paths.
If one can know things as they truly are, one relies on non-duality and is liberated.
Not delighting in the grasping at existence or non-existence, because of having discerned the true meaning,
if one falls into non-grasping, why would you not say that one has fallen into existence?
If you say that by refuting existence, one falls into non-existence because the logical consequence follows,
then why does such a refutation of non-existence not likewise fall into existence?
Since there is no speech or mind, it is because of relying upon bodhi.
If you say that they fall into non-existence, for what reason do they not fall into existence?
The Sāṃkhyas, the Vaiśeṣikas, and the Nirgranthas speak of the person and the aggregates;
regarding these worldly conventions, you ask them: "If you say they transcend both existence and non-existence," [how can you maintain your position?]
This is an ineffable dharma, for it transcends existence and non-existence.
You should know this profound nectar of the Buddha’s true teaching:
like the dawn, it has no coming or going, nor does it abide for even a single moment.
If the substance transcends the three times, in which time could it be said to exist substantially?
The two times [past and future] lack going and coming, and the present does not truly abide.
How can these statements—that there is the arising, abiding, and ceasing of the times—be real?
If there were constant change, what phenomenon would not perish moment by moment?
If there were no perishing moment by moment, how could there be change?
If one says there is perishing moment by moment, it is because [the entity] perishes both partially and in its entirety.
Because they are not perceived simultaneously, these two [theories] are illogical.
If the mind perishes upon every thought, how can there be a "former object"?
If the mind were firm and did not perish, how could a "former object" be established?
Just as there is a posterior limit to a moment, so too are there prior and middle limits;
because a moment has three parts, the world and its thoughts do not abide.
Since a single thought possesses these three limits, one should discern the limits in the same way as one discerns the thought.
The three periods of past, present, and future are not established through themselves or others.
Because they do not consist of a single momentary part, if there were no parts, how could they exist?
Apart from the one, what is the multiplicity?
Apart from existence, what dharma could there be that is non-existent?
Through cessation and through counteraction— if one says that existence becomes non-existence,
then regarding this non-existence and its counteraction, by virtue of what dharma would there be existence or non-existence?
Therefore, both the world and nirvāṇa do not exist as entities in reality;
when others asked the Buddha about the existence of a future limit to the world, he remained silent.
Because he is the Honored One of All-Knowledge, the wise recognize him as such.
Because of this profound Dharma, it is not taught to those who are not suitable vessels.
Such a dharma of liberation is profoundly deep and free from all attachments;
therefore, the Buddhas, with their omniscience, declare it to be without foundation or bottom.
Regarding the dharma that is free from dependence and attachment, it transcends the two extremes of existence and non-existence.
Worldly people, however, accept dependence and attachment; due to delusion, they are struck with fear and lose [the truth].
Thus, they ruin themselves and others, fearing a state of non-reliance.
O King, may you remain unshakable; do not let yourself be destroyed by that [delusion].
To bring about your indestructibility, I shall proclaim the True Principle.
By relying on the non-erroneous union and abandoning the dualistic grasping at existence and non-existence, [you shall attain it].
This transcends merit and demerit; its profound meaning is clearly manifest.
It is not for those terrified of emptiness by the view of a self; it should be taught as the domain of two types of persons.
The four great elements, space, and consciousness—this single aggregate is not a person.
If the person does not exist in either combination or separation, how can one grasp at the existence of a person?
Just as the six elements are not the person—being a mere collection, they are empty and not real—so it is with each individual element; because they are a collection, they are not real.
The aggregates (skandhas) are neither the self nor belong to the self; apart from the aggregates, no self is manifest.
It is not like fire mixed with fuel; how then could the self be established in dependence on the aggregates?
The earth element is not the other three great elements, nor are the three present within the earth.
Among the three, earth does not exist; they cannot be established apart from one another.
The great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind do not each exist by way of their own intrinsic nature;
one is not established apart from the other three, and likewise, the three are not established apart from the one.
If one, three, and thirty do not exist apart from one another, they cannot each exist individually;
how then could they exist in separation? If they were established independently of one another, why would there be no fire apart from fuel?
Motion, obstruction, and aggregation—so too it is with water, wind, and earth.
If fire does not establish itself independently, how can the other three be established individually?
Regarding the principle that the three great elements arise through conditions, how could they be established if they were mutually contradictory?
If those [elements] were each established independently, how could they exist in mutual dependence?
If they were not established independently, how could they exist through mutual dependence?
If you say that the great elements are established independently yet are not separate from one another, [this is untenable].
If they are not mixed, they do not coexist; if they are mixed, they do not exist independently.
Since the great elements are not established individually, how can they have individual intrinsic natures?
They are established individually without one being more prevalent than another; therefore, their characteristics are spoken of as conventional designations.
Visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles; the analysis of their meaning is like the Great [Vehicle].
Eye, visible forms, consciousness, and ignorance; the analysis of karma and birth is likewise so.
Agent, karma, and activity; number, conjunction, cause, effect, and time.
Shortness and length, as well as names and concepts, and likewise non-conceptualization and discernment;
earth, water, wind, fire, and the like; long and short, small and large;
good and evil, speech, consciousness, and knowledge—all these are extinguished without remainder within wisdom.
Just as the sphere of consciousness is formless, boundless, and pervasive of all,
so too within it the elements such as earth and the rest are entirely extinguished.
Within this wisdom of signlessness, there are neither long nor short, neither good nor evil karmas.
Name-and-form and the aggregates— these cease without remainder in this way.
Just as it is with consciousness, because these previously existed due to ignorance,
once wisdom arises regarding consciousness, all of these subsequently come to an end.
Such worldly phenomena as these are the fuel for the fire of consciousness;
by means of the light of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the fuel of worldly consciousness is consumed.
Through the discernment of existence and non-existence apart from delusion, one subsequently discriminates true suchness (*tathatā*).
Since existence cannot be found upon investigation, how can non-existence be attained?
Because it is constituted by formlessness, emptiness is merely a name;
apart from the great elements, what constitutes form?
Therefore, form is also merely a name;
feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness should be contemplated as being like the four great elements.
As the four great elements are empty of a self, so too the six elements are neither person nor dharma.
Just as when a plantain tree is dissected part by part, nothing remains and it is found to be non-existent;
so too, when a person is analyzed according to the six elements, they are entirely empty.
Therefore, the Buddha has correctly taught that all phenomena are without self.
The six elements alone are designated as "dharmas," and it is definitively determined that they lack a self.
When one examines the two meanings of "self" and "non-self" according to reality, neither can be found;
therefore, the Tathāgata negates both extremes of self and non-self.

The terms "seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing" are taught by the Buddha to be neither real nor unreal, for these two are established through mutual dependence; thus, these two do not exist in reality.
When examining the world according to reality, one transcends both the real and the unreal.
Thus, the world relies on reality, and therefore falls into existence and non-existence.
If phenomena are everywhere not as they appear, how could the Buddha have taught that there is finitude or infinity, duality or non-duality?
The Buddhas of the past are immeasurable; those of the present and future exceed all calculation.
Beyond the limit of the realms of sentient beings, the three periods of time are manifested by the Buddha.
There is no cause for the world’s duration; this limit is manifested in relation to the world.
The world transcends existence and non-existence; how then could the Buddha predict its limits?
Because the Dharma is so profound, he kept it secret from the common folk and did not speak of it.
To teach that the world is like an illusion or a magical transformation—this is the Buddha’s nectar-like teaching.
Just as in the case of a magically conjured image, Arising and ceasing can still be perceived;
yet when this image and its arising and ceasing Are examined for their ultimate reality, they are found not to exist.
The world is like a magical illusion; Thus, its arising and ceasing may be seen.
The world and its arising and ceasing, when examined according to their true meaning, are all empty.
Like a magical illusion, they have no place from which they come, nor any place to which they go;
it is only the deluded minds of sentient beings that, due to [clinging to] reality, do not abide.
If the nature of the world transcends the three times, how can the world be real?
Who speaks of existence or non-existence?
Existence and non-existence are ultimately without meaning.
Therefore, the Buddha, regarding the four propositions, did not provide a definitive teaching on the world;
for both existence and non-existence are empty, and this emptiness itself is neither empty nor non-empty.
This body is characterized by impurity and is the sphere of coarse realized wisdom.
Even that which is constantly and repeatedly seen does not enter and abide within the mind;
how much more so the True Dharma, which is subtle, profound, and without bottom or foundation?
It is difficult to realize with a distracted mind—how could it be easily entered?
Therefore, when the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he declined to preach and intended to enter nirvana,
because he saw that this True Dharma was so profound as to be difficult to understand.
If the Dharma is not correctly realized, it will harm those who lack intelligence.
By grasping this incorrectly, one falls into the foul pit of false views.
When a person’s understanding of the Dharma is unclear, they exalt themselves and disparage the Dharma;
by giving rise to slander, they destroy themselves, falling headlong into hell.
Just as with excellent food and drink, using them excessively brings danger;
yet by eating according to the proper measure, one gains long life, strength, and happiness.
If one understands the True Dharma in a biased way, the encounter with suffering is just like this.
If one can understand according to reality, one will experience happiness and awakening.
When a wise person abandons slander and false attachments toward the True Dharma and applies themselves to right knowledge, they thereby accomplish their aspirations.
Because one does not understand this Dharma, people give rise to the long-standing view of self;
because of this, they create the three types of karma, and subsequently are born in the good or evil realms.
Until one realizes the Dharma that can utterly extinguish the view of self, [the cycle continues].
Always reverently arouse right effort in regard to morality, generosity, patience, and so forth.
Let the Dharma be foremost in your actions, and let the Dharma be present in the middle and at the end—
meaning that which is the truth without falsehood— and thus you shall not sink in this life or the next.
Because of the Dharma, one gains a good reputation; At the time of death, one is happy and free from fear;
In future lives, one receives wealth and joy. Therefore, one should always serve the Dharma.
Only the Dharma is the correct governance; Through the Dharma, the whole world holds one dear.
If a ruler inspires the love of his people, he will not be deceived in this life;
if he governs by what is contrary to the Dharma, the ruler will meet with the aversion of his ministers,
and due to the world’s hatred, he will find no joy in this life.
To deceive others through royal law is a great peril and an evil path;
how can such evil wisdom and false livelihood be called right?
If a person is solely intent on deceiving others, how can their actions be said to be right?
Therefore, throughout ten thousand lifetimes, one will constantly suffer the deceptions of others.
If you wish to cause your enemies grief, abandon their faults and adopt their virtues;
through this, your own benefit will be perfected, and you will thereby cause your enemies to suffer in sorrow and distress.
Through generosity and kind speech, through beneficial conduct and shared purpose,
may you gather in the world and thereby propagate the True Dharma.
O King, if you speak with one word of truth, the people will place firm faith in you.
This is like the false speech of the Honored One, which does not give rise to the trust of others.
When the sincere mind arises without contradiction, flowing smoothly to benefit others, this is called truthful speech; the opposite of this is called false speech.
If one’s renunciation of wealth is clear, it can conceal the king’s faults;
yet such a lord who is stingy with his bounty can destroy the king’s many virtues.
If a king stills all evils, his virtue will be profound and he will be loved and honored by the people.
Therefore, having been taught by the Vidyārāja, one should practice tranquility.
Because the King of Wisdom is unshakable, one understands for oneself and does not rely on others;
thus never being deceived, one should resolutely cultivate wisdom.
Relying on the truths, renunciation, tranquility, and wisdom, the King possesses these four virtues;
like the True Dharma with its four qualities, he is praised by gods and humans.
Able to subdue others and proclaim purity, he is stainless through his wisdom and compassion.
Constantly associating with the wise causes royal law and wisdom to grow.
A person who speaks well is hard to find, and one who listens to virtuous words is likewise rare;
yet the third kind of person is most excellent—one who can swiftly act upon good instruction.
If a wholesome deed is not yet beloved, one should know it and practice it swiftly;
just as a medicine may have a bitter taste, one should take it with determination for the sake of recovery.
Regarding longevity, health, and royal power, one should constantly contemplate their impermanence.
Next, one should conceive the thought of revulsion and fear; thereafter, one should practice the Dharma with single-minded devotion.
Seeing that death is certain and that suffering follows from evil views at the time of death, the wise person seeks happiness in the present; therefore, they should not commit sinful deeds.
If one sees no fear in a single moment, yet sees fear in a later time, and if the mind is at peace for that one moment, why would one not be fearless later?
Through alcohol, one encounters the contempt of others; it ruins affairs and diminishes physical strength.
Because acting contrary to what is right arises from delusion, the wise person abandons alcohol.
Games such as chess and other diversions give rise to greed, hatred, anxiety, and deceit;
they are the causes of falsehood and harsh speech, and therefore one should always remain far removed from them.
The fault of lustful indulgence arises from perceiving the female body as pure;
yet when one investigates the female body, not even a single hair’s breadth of purity is found there.
A woman’s mouth is a vessel for saliva and spittle, and her teeth and tongue are foul with grime and impurity.
The nose is foul from the flow of mucus; the eyes are the seat of tears;
the belly is a vessel for excrement, urine, and intestines; the rest of the body is a heap of flesh and bone.
Fools are deluded by this loathsome thing, and thus they cling greedily to it.
The gates of the sense-faculties are most foul and impure; they are the cause for aversion toward the body.
If one conceives craving for them, by what means can one become free from desire?
They are like a vessel for excrement and urine, yet the pig delights in playing within it.
Regarding the impure gateways of the body, so too are many desires and play.
The reason these gateways arise is to discard the filth of the bodily soil;
yet foolish people, through perverse attachment, disregard their own true benefit.
You yourself see one part of it—the impurities such as feces and urine—and this collection is called the "body. How can you give rise to attachment toward it?
Red and white serve as the seeds of birth; it is nourished by being drenched with the filth of the latrine.
If one knows the body is impure, why does suffering give rise to craving?
This loathsome collection of filth, wrapped in stinking, moist skin—
if one can lie within it, then one will be attached to a woman’s body.
Whether it be lovely or loathsome, whether aged or a young maiden, the female body is entirely impure; where, then, do you give rise to desire?
Even if a heap of excrement were beautiful in color, soft, smooth, and well-proportioned, [it would still be foul].
To give rise to craving is improper; the same applies to the body of a woman.
Internally it is foul and utterly impure, concealed only by an outer skin;
being of the nature of a corpse, how can one look upon it and not recognize this?
The skin is as impure as a garment; it cannot be briefly removed for washing.
How then can this skin, a mere heap of filth, be temporarily cleansed by artifice?
Like a painted jar filled with excrement, if you loathe its outward decoration, [why do you not reject the vessel itself?]
This body is filled with impurities; why do you not feel weary of it?
If you loathe what is unclean, why do you not abhor this body?
Fragrant flowers, garlands, food, and drink—though pure in their origin, they can defile it.
Just as you simultaneously loathe the filth of yourself and others,
why do you not feel revulsion for your own and others' impure bodies?
As the female body is impure, so too is one's own body defiled.
Therefore, one who has abandoned desire is inwardly and outwardly harmonious.
Though impurity flows from the nine gates, they personally realize and wash it away themselves.
If one does not know this impurity yet composes treatises on sensual love, [they are deluded].
How rare is this extreme ignorance, this lack of shame and contempt for others!
Toward this most impure body, how can it possibly benefit you?
Because of this, many sentient beings have their minds shrouded by nescience.
Bound by the fetters of sensual desire, they struggle like dogs fighting over dung.
As scratching an itch is called pleasure, yet being itch-free is the greatest bliss;
so too, while those with desire have their pleasures, the person free from desire has the supreme bliss.
If you contemplate this meaning, detachment from desire cannot be achieved;
because you contemplate desire as light, you will not encounter the fault of sexual indulgence.
From hunting one experiences a short lifespan, and through the fear of suffering, one is heavily oppressed by affliction.
Since one will certainly undergo this in the future, one should therefore practice compassion with firm resolve.
Should anyone else see it, they would be struck with extreme terror,
as if seeing a foul and filthy body from which poisonous, wicked snakes are streaming forth.
When this person arrives there, sentient beings will attain peace and happiness,
just as farmers see the great clouds of summer month and long for rain. Therefore,
you should abandon unwholesome dharmas and resolve to cultivate wholesome conduct.
In order that both self and others may attain the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi—
this root of bodhi consists of a mind as firm as the king of mountains,
compassion reaching to the limits of the ten directions, and non-dual dependent wisdom.
Great King, listen attentively; I shall now explain the causes that have brought about the thirty-two marks capable of adorning your body.
By making offerings to and constantly attending upon the Caityas and the Noble Ones, [you have attained these marks].
With the precious marks of wheels upon his hands and feet, he shall become a Wheel-Turning King;
his hands and feet are smooth and soft, and his body has seven prominent parts—
due to having bestowed excellent food and drink, he has brought others to equal abundance.
Your body shall be perfectly formed and upright, with fingers and heels that are rounded and long;
you shall attain a long life because you compassionately saved a condemned prisoner.
O Great King, uphold the Dharma firmly so that it may remain pure for a long time.
By this, his feet will be level and firm, and he shall become a Bodhisattva.
Through practicing generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation,
his fingers and toes will be webbed and his hands and feet will possess eighty auspicious marks.
The ankles are high and lovely; the hair of the whorls points upward.
Because he did not abandon his long-held practice, this is the dharma originally received and maintained.
Through respectful giving and receiving, as well as the fields of knowledge and the arts, [he attained these marks].
Therefore, I have attained the calves of a deer-king, as well as intelligence and great wisdom.
When others sought what was my own possession, I was able to bestow it upon them swiftly;
by this, my arms became long and powerful, and I attained the status of a World Teacher.
When loved ones are separated, the Bodhisattva brings them together in harmony;
this brings about the mark of the concealed organ, as he is ever clothed in the raiment of shame.
Constantly bestowing palatial mansions and the finest, soft, and lovely colors, [he attains these marks].
Therefore, he manifested a celestial body, smooth, supple, and subtly radiant.
By practicing supreme protection and acting in accordance with principle toward his elders,
he attained the mark of a single pore per hair, and a face adorned with the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows.
He constantly speaks words that are kind and loving, and is further able to accord with the true teaching.
His upper body is like that of a lion, and his neck is rounded like a *mṛdvīkā* grape.
He tends to the sick and provides them with medicine, or else causes others to provide such care and protection.
Therefore, his armpits are full, and he can distinguish a hundred flavors with a single pulse.
In matters concerning the Dharma for himself and others, he is always able to serve as their leader.
His cranial protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) is prominent, and his jaw is broad and well-proportioned.
By speaking skillfully for a long time with words that are truly beautiful, smooth,
and virtuous, one attains the eightfold Brahma-voice as well as a long and broad tongue.
Having understood the facts and their benefits, one repeatedly teaches them to others.
One who is well-born like a lion has a countenance most worthy of love.
Because they honor others and do not treat them with contempt, and because they act in accordance with the true principle,
their teeth will be white and even, surpassing all others like a string of genuine pearls.
By repeatedly practicing this speech— speaking truthfully and refraining from double-tongued talk—
one possesses forty teeth that are smooth, firm, strong, and pure.
By gazing upon sentient beings with a mind free from greed, hatred, and delusion, one’s gaze is gentle and serene.
The pupils of your eyes are clear and lustrous, and your eyelids are like those of a bull-king.
From this brief description of the marks of a Great Man and their causes,
you should know that you are a Bodhisattva, a Wheel-Turning King, beautifully adorned.
There are eighty secondary marks, which flow forth from compassion;
Great King, I do not describe them here to avoid excessive verbiage.
Although all universal monarchs possess these same marks and excellencies, [the Buddha's are distinct].
Though pure, radiant, and lovely, they can never equal the Tathāgata.
Even a single fraction of a single thought-moment of a Bodhisattva’s virtuous mind cannot be equaled by the causes for the marks and signs of a Wheel-Turning King.
Even if one person were to cultivate roots of goodness for ten trillion eons,
they would not produce even a single causal condition for a single pore-mark of a Buddha.
A portion of the marks of all Buddhas is equal to that of a wheel-turning monarch.
Just as a firefly and the sun have a slight resemblance in their light,
so it is with the great marks and signs of the Buddhas, which arise from inconceivable merit.
I shall now explain them for you, based upon the Mahāyāna Abhidharma.
The merit of all pratyekabuddhas, the merit of those in training and those beyond training,
and the merit of all beings in the ten directions— merit such as this is difficult to measure in the world.
Ten times this merit would produce a single pore-mark of a Buddha.
Ninety-nine thousand hairs, each and every one possessing such merit;
through such vast accumulations of merit, all the hairs of a Buddha are produced.
When this merit is increased a hundredfold again, it then brings forth a single secondary mark of a Buddha.
In this way, and in this way, many [merits], each one well-accomplished,
even up to eighty, adorn a single major mark.
Such a mass of merit is able to evoke the eighty secondary marks.
When multiplied again by a hundredfold, it brings about one of the Buddha’s major marks.
Through such vast merit, he can bring about thirty of these marks;
when multiplied yet again by a hundredfold, it brings about the ūrṇā-kośa, which resembles the full moon.
The merit capable of producing the white tuft of hair increases again a thousandfold;
the merit that produces the invisible *ūrṇā* on the crown of the head is likewise immeasurable.
Though such merit is infinite, it is explained through skillful means as being finite.
Throughout all the ten directions, as it is said, worlds are tenfold;
even the causes for the form-bodies (*rūpakāya*) of the Buddhas are as immeasurable as these worlds,
so how could there be any limit to the causes for their Dharma-bodies (*dharmakāya*)?
In the world, though causes may be small, if their fruits are great, they are difficult to measure;
since the causes of the Buddhas are immeasurable, how can one conceive of the magnitude of their fruits?
The physical bodies of all Buddhas arise entirely from meritorious deeds.
Great King, the Buddha’s Dharma-body is accomplished through the practice of wisdom;
therefore, the Buddha’s practices of merit and wisdom are the direct cause of enlightenment.
Thus, I pray that you will always practice these meritorious and wise deeds of enlightenment.
Regarding the merit of attaining enlightenment, do not fall into deep sorrow;
through reasoning and the *āśaya*, you can cause your mind to find peace and faith.
Just as the ten directions are boundless, so too are space and the elements of earth, water, and fire.
Those sentient beings who suffer, they are likewise infinite.
These infinite sentient beings, the Bodhisattva, relying on great compassion,
delivers from suffering and vows that they may attain parinirvāṇa.
From the moment this firm resolve was made, whether walking, standing, lying down, or awake,
even if one were occasionally slightly negligent, an immeasurable flow of merit would constantly stream forth.
As vast as the number of sentient beings, this merit flows perpetually without interruption.
Since cause and effect are thus commensurate, enlightenment is not difficult to attain.
Regarding the time, sentient beings, enlightenment itself, and merit—
through these four immeasurables, the bodhisattva practices with a steadfast mind.
Although bodhi is immeasurable, because one cultivates the two practices of merit and wisdom by means of the four immeasurables, how could it be difficult to attain?
These two types of practice, merit and wisdom, are thus without limit.
Because the Bodhisattva’s body and mind suffer, their ailments are swiftly eliminated.
The hunger, thirst, and other such physical sufferings of the evil realms arise from evil karma;
the Bodhisattva is forever free from evil, and thus suffering does not arise as they practice virtue.
Desire, hatred, fear, and the like—mental suffering arises from delusion;
by relying on non-dual wisdom, the bodhisattva is free from mental suffering.
When suffering exists for even a brief moment, it is difficult to endure, how much more so when it is prolonged?
When there is no suffering, time is long; when there is joy, how could it be difficult?
Physical suffering never exists for them, yet they speak metaphorically of mental suffering.
Out of compassion for the world’s two kinds of suffering, they thus dwell eternally in saṃsāra.
Therefore, though the path to enlightenment is long, the wise do not sink in spirit;
to extinguish evil and give rise to good, they practice without interruption at this time.
May you recognize and abandon greed, hatred, and ignorance.
One should know that the various virtues, such as non-attachment and the rest, ought to be cultivated with reverence.
From attachment one is born into the realm of hungry ghosts; from hatred one falls into hell;
from delusion one enters the animal realm. By reversing these, one attains rebirth among humans and devas.
Abandoning evil and cultivating good—this dharma is the cause of happiness.
If it is the dharma of liberation, one abandons the two attachments through wisdom.
Buddha images and reliquaries (caityas), as well as halls and monasteries.
With the most excellent and abundant offerings, you should reverently prepare them.
Seated upon a precious lotus flower, beautifully colored and exquisitely painted,
with every kind of gold and jewel, you should fashion an image of the Buddha.
The True Dharma and the Noble Assembly, protected by his life, form, and wealth;
with nets of gold and jewels and parasols, he made offerings to cover the *caityas*.
With flowers of gold, silver, and various gems, as well as coral, beryl, and pearls.
Śakra, Mahāśyāma, Vajrapāṇi, and the caitya;
those who can preach the Dharma of the True Person— these one should honor with the four requisites,
and constantly and diligently practice such dharmas as the six points of respectful harmony.
Listen with reverence to the Honored One; serve and protect him with diligence—this is what a Bodhisattva must practice, and continue to offer worship even after his passing.
One should not personally serve or pay homage to those outside the fold, such as the followers of non-Buddhist paths.
Due to ignorance and false faith, do not serve evil associates.
Copy, read, recite, and offer the Buddha’s Āgamas and Śāstras;
likewise, bestow paper, pens, and ink—this is the merit you should cultivate.
He established schools throughout the land, hiring teachers and providing for scholars;
he founded enduring foundations so that your conduct might bring forth long-lasting wisdom.
He mastered medicine and skillful mathematics, and for all these, he provided fields and lands.
He moistened the suffering of the aged, the young, and the sick, providing relief and benefit to the nation.
He established various monasteries, as well as gardens, ponds, lakes, pavilions, and dwellings;
therein he provided the necessities of life—mats of grass, bedding, food and drink, and firewood.
In small and great kingdoms, one should establish monasteries, pavilions, and guesthouses;
for those on distant roads who lack water and drink, one should construct wells and ponds to provide sustenance.
For those suffering from illness, the destitute, those of low birth, the fearful, and others alike—[one should provide for them].
Out of compassion and with a mind of diligent care, establish others [in virtue].
Regarding fresh food and drink, fruits, vegetables, and new grains—
whether for the great assembly or for those in need— one must not consume them before they have been offered.
Shoes, umbrellas, water flasks, hooks, tweezers, needles, thread, fans, and the like;
mats, bedding, and resting gear—these should be offered to monasteries, pavilions, and guest houses.
The three fruits and the three pungent spices, honey, molasses, ghee, and eye medicine.
One should always provide rest-houses with written spells and medicinal prescriptions;
medicinal oils for anointing the head and body, basins for washing, lamps, parched grain,
fruit, water vessels, and knives and axes should be supplied within these pavilions.
Rice, grain, hemp, food, and drink, along with sugar, ghee, and related items,
should always be kept in a cool, shaded place, as well as vessels filled with pure water.
At the entrances of ant and rat holes, one should provide food, grain, sugar, and the like.
I pray that you may cause trustworthy persons to distribute [offerings] daily;
May they provide food as desired, both before and after meals, Constantly bestowing it upon hungry ghosts,
dogs, rats, birds, ants, and the like— I pray that you will constantly provide such food.
During times of pestilence and famine, of drought, flood, and the perils of bandits;
when the nation is in ruin and requires deliverance—may you ever provide relief and succor.
When farmers are cut off from their agricultural work, may you grant them grain, seeds, and all necessary implements.
At the appropriate times, remit rents and taxes; levy light and modest assessments.
Bestow goods to relieve the poor and those in debt; interest shall not be excessive or harsh.
Allow for rest and relaxation as needed; receive guests according to the season.
Robberies within and without the realm were suppressed through skillful means until they ceased;
caravans were dispatched according to the season, and commodity prices were regulated and balanced.
When the eight high ministers adjudicated affairs, they examined them with impartiality and reason.
If one’s deeds can benefit the myriad people, one should always practice with reverence.
What should one do for one's own benefit?
Reflect upon this with constant respect, as you have done.
How is the benefit of others accomplished?
Reflect on this with urgency.
Earth, water, wind, fire, and so forth, as well as medicinal herbs and wild trees—
Thus, even for a brief moment, receiving the unimpeded exhortation of another,
one gives rise to the thought of relinquishing both internal and external wealth;
the merit of such a Bodhisattva is accomplished as immeasurable as space.
A young maiden, lovely and adorned, who practices generosity for those who seek it,
shall therefore obtain dhāraṇī and be able to uphold all dharmas.
One who loves beauty and possesses full adornment, along with all the necessities of life—
In the past, Śākyamuni Buddha bestowed eighty thousand young maidens;
with light of various colors, robes, ornaments, flowers, incense,
and other such things, he gave to supplicants in accordance with compassion and wisdom.
If a person lacks these conditions and cannot practice the Dharma with stability, one should give to them; beyond this, do not bestow [the teaching].
Even poison may be given to such a person, provided that it can benefit others.
Amṛta is not permitted to be given if it would cause harm to another.
Even if a snake bites a person’s finger, the Buddha allows its removal;
for when the Buddha’s teaching is for the benefit of others, even what causes distress may be practiced.
One should firmly and reverently uphold the True Dharma, as well as those who can preach it;
listen to and receive the Dharma with respect, or give the Dharma as a gift to others.
Do not crave worldly praise, but always delight in the supramundane Dharma.
Just as one establishes one's own essential qualities, so should one act toward others.
Never be satisfied with mere hearing; rather, contemplate and cultivate the true meaning.
In repaying the kindness of the teacher, one should practice respect without stinginess.
Do not read heterodox or evil treatises, for they only give rise to contention and pride;
do not praise your own virtues, yet you may praise the virtues of others, even those who harbor enmity toward you.
Do not disclose the secrets of others, nor engage in malicious double-tongued speech.
When one has committed a fault against another, one should examine it according to reason and confess it with remorse.
If, because of such a transgression, a wise person reproaches another, one must personally abandon that fault;
only then will one have the capacity to rescue and deliver others.
When others insult you, do not be angry; instead, contemplate your own past evil karma.
Do not retaliate with evil toward them, so that you may not suffer in the future.
You should show kindness to others, and do not hope for their repayment.
One should experience suffering alone; seek happiness together with the multitude.
If you attain great wealth and status, do not act with self-exaltation.
When encountering injustice like a hungry ghost, do not give rise to base or sorrowful conduct.
Even if one were to lose their royal throne, or even die because of speaking the truth, one should always speak such words; if there is no benefit in truth, remain silent.
As it is said, "Act accordingly," may you firmly practice what is wholesome.
Therefore, when one's good reputation is widespread, one achieves sovereign authority as a valid measure.
One should apply diligent discernment and subsequently act in accordance with reason;
do not act out of mere faith in others, but must personally realize the true meaning.
If one practices virtue in accordance with principle, a good reputation will spread throughout the ten directions;
kings and lords will continue in succession, and royal wealth and joy will increase ever greater.
The conditions for death are of a hundred kinds, while the causes for longevity are few.
Since these causes may become conditions for death, one should always practice virtue.
If a person constantly performs virtuous deeds, the peace and happiness thereby obtained will be equal toward both self and others; such virtuous happiness is perfect and complete.
For one whose nature is established in the Dharma, sleep and waking are always peaceful and joyful;
they see auspicious things in their dreams because there is no fault or evil within.
If a person supports their parents and reverently honors their elders at home, [they shall attain such bliss].
Respectfully serve virtuous people and use wealth for their sake; practice patience with great magnanimity.
Speak gentle words and refrain from double-tongued speech; speak truthfully, and you will find joy in living together.
These are the causes for becoming a Deva King of the Nine Heavens; one should practice them throughout one's entire life.
By practicing nine dharmas in the past, the Lord of Devas attained the imperial throne;
from time to time, residing in the Hall of Dharma, he has constantly preached this until now.
Three times each day he bestowed three hundred vessels of exquisite food.
The merit of this does not equal even a single moment of practicing loving-kindness by even one percent.

Protected by gods and humans alike, one experiences joy day and night, and is spared from the fire of enmity, poison, and the staff of punishment; these are the manifest fruits of practicing loving-kindness.
One obtains wealth without effort and is later reborn in the form realm,
attaining the ten merits of loving-kindness.
If one has not yet attained liberation, one should teach all sentient beings to firmly resolve upon the bodhicitta.
The Bodhisattva’s virtue is like a mountain; the bodhicitta is firm and stable.
Through faith, one leaves the eight difficulties behind; through precepts, one is born in the good realms.
By frequently cultivating the emptiness of true thusness, one attains goodness and remains free from negligence.
Through freedom from flattery, one attains the faculty of mindfulness; through constant reflection, one attains the faculty of wisdom.
Through reverence, one masters the meaning and principles; by protecting the Dharma, one gains the recollection of past lives.
By practicing generosity and hearing the Dharma—or by not obstructing others from hearing it—[one attains these fruits].
One will swiftly attain what is cherished, And encounter the Buddha face to face.
By being free from greed, one’s undertakings succeed; By not being stingy with wealth, it increases.
By abandoning pride, one invites the highest grade [of rebirth]; Through patience in the Dharma, one attains dhāraṇī.
By practicing the five kinds of giving and bestowing fearlessness, one cannot be humiliated by any insults; thus, one attains great and supreme power.
By performing the practice of offering rows of lamps at caityas and holding torches in the deep darkness, [one gains such strength].
By offering oil for the continuity of light, one attains the pure divine eye;
When making offerings at a caitya, by providing the sound of drums and music,
And the exquisite tones of conchs, horns, and so forth, one obtains the pure divine ear.
Remaining silent regarding the faults of others, not speaking of their virtues or deficiencies,
and acting in accordance with them to protect their minds— by these means, one attains the knowledge of others' minds.
By giving boats and vehicles to transport those who are weak and exhausted, [one gains mastery over the elements].
By reverently gazing upon one's elders, one attains the supernormal power of psychic travel (ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna).
By causing others to remember Dharma matters, as well as the words and meanings of the True Dharma,
or by giving the Dharma with a pure mind, one brings forth the knowledge of past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna).
Through knowing the true meaning—that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature—one attains the sixth supernormal power, which is supreme: the exhaustion of the outflows.
This is conjoined with impartial compassion, arising from the cultivation of wisdom as it truly is.
Thus, having attained Buddhahood for oneself, one constantly liberates sentient beings.
Through various pure vows, the Buddha-land is purified;
by offering various jewels to the caityas, boundless light is emitted.
Thus, having understood that these actions and their fruits are consistent with the ultimate meaning, one should cultivate the benefit of others; this is itself the Bodhisattva’s self-benefit.
If a king acts contrary to the Dharma or conducts himself unreasonably, [the people will suffer].
Even those who serve the king praise him; thus, his likes and dislikes are difficult to discern.
There are people in the world who do not love virtue and are hard to instruct;
how much more so for a great king—how could he accept the words of virtuous men?
Out of compassion for you now, and out of pity for all the world, I instruct you well;
though it may not be pleasant, it is truly beneficial.
It is genuine, smooth, and meaningful, delivered at the proper time through loving-kindness and compassion.
The Buddha commanded that his disciples be instructed; therefore, I shall speak for you.
If you listen to these true words, you should abide in freedom from anger.
You should accept what must be received, just as one takes pure water when bathing.
I now speak these virtuous words, which bring benefit in both the present and the future;
you should know them and practice them for your own sake and for the sake of the world.
Because you gave alms to the poor and suffering in the past, you have now experienced the resulting wealth and riches.
Due to greed, one fails to recognize kindness; by neglecting generosity, one shall not obtain more.
In this world, there is only the provisions for the journey; if one does not hire, no one will carry the load.
By giving even a small portion through charity, one shall bear a hundredfold burden in the future.
May you give rise to the great mind and constantly undertake great deeds;
if one acts with the mind of a great task, such a person shall attain the great fruit.
A king of small intent and narrow capacity has never even touched the aspiration for the mind [of enlightenment].
A good reputation and auspicious matters should be pursued by relying upon the Three Jewels.
Even if you were to lose the hair of the King or Queen, if the matter is contrary to your dharma,
death will bring ill repute, and the King will not be the most excellent.
A great undertaking can thus be initiated; it is a rare application for a Great Man, yet it obstructs the aspirations of inferior persons. He accomplished this matter at the cost of his life;
having no possessions to call his own, he entered the future alone.
If one deposits wealth in the Dharma, it will meet one with a welcoming embrace when one arrives before [death].
The various properties of a former emperor are abandoned by their original owner and belong to the new king;
yet can they produce for the former king the joy of the Dharma and a good reputation?
Using wealth brings joy in the present; giving it away brings happiness in the future.
These two are not in vain; otherwise, one produces only suffering and no joy.
When one wishes to practice giving at the time of death, ministers obstruct one and cause the loss of autonomy.
Since the royal lineage has been severed, he has abandoned his affection and follows the desires of the new king.
If you were to renounce all worldly things, you could now propagate the Dharma in peace;
yet you remain constantly subject to the conditions of death, like a lamp in the wind.
May the temples of the gods, which were previously established by former kings as places of merit for all, be restored and maintained just as they were.
Abandoning killing, always practice virtue; uphold the precepts and cherish those who have served you long.
Skillfully increasing wealth without contention, Diligently and constantly cultivating virtue;
Pure and without accumulation, Not neglecting the welfare of others,
Established as a leader, One receives that treasury of merit.
The blind, those with diseased organs, and the physically impaired—pitiable and without refuge—they must not be turned away at a temple; give them food with impartiality.
Those who seek neither worldly gain nor spiritual merit, even if they dwell in the realm of another king, [should likewise be provided for].
The service should likewise be similar; one should act without distinction between "this" and "that.
Regarding all matters of the Dharma, one should appoint a person who is diligent, free from greed, intelligent, wise, virtuous, non-intrusive toward the Dharma, and fearful of transgression.
One who understands right treatises and practices goodness, whose four types of observation regarding loved ones are pure,
whose speech is beautiful and not timid, and who is of noble lineage and able to uphold the precepts;
one who recognizes kindness, knows the suffering of others, and possesses skillful discernment according to principle— [such a person is truly wise].
These eight men were mutually ashamed [of their own faults], and for the sake of the state, they established the eight seats of office.
Gentle and flexible with great magnanimity, they possessed courage and were deeply devoted to the king;
steadfast and capable of managing wealth, they were ever virtuous and free from negligence.
One who has carefully considered the affairs to be undertaken, can distinguish the twelve wheels, and constantly practices the four skillful means— such a person should be appointed as a minister.
One who upholds the Dharma and precepts with purity, understands affairs, and possesses administrative capability, [should be appointed].
One who can grow and protect wealth, understands meaning, and is skilled in writing and calculation;
who is impartial toward the affairs of others, fears transgression, loves the king,
possesses abundant riches and many followers— such a person is fit to be appointed to office.
Month after month, one should inquire of him regarding all income and expenditure of wealth;
as for inquiries concerning one's own religious affairs and the like, he should instruct and admonish with a joyful heart.
One should occupy the royal throne for the sake of the Dharma, seeking neither fame nor the dust of sensual desires.
The sovereignty of kingship is supremely beneficial; nothing else compares to it.
Great King, in this world, beings mostly devour one another.
Establish the principle of royal sovereignty, and listen attentively as I explain it to you.
The elders in the king’s court, being of noble lineage and discerning right from wrong, act with great conformity out of fear of evil; may they attend to the king’s affairs.
As for punishments such as imprisonment, flogging, and caning, if they carry them out according to principle, [the realm will be well-ordered].
The King’s great compassion is ever-flowing; he bestows further grace upon them.
For the benefit of all people, he should constantly give rise to a heart of loving-kindness;
even toward those who commit the most grievous evils, he should likewise give rise to great compassion.
Even toward one with a mind of grave evil and extreme malice, one must surely practice compassion;
such a person is a vessel for compassion and the proper object of the practitioner’s mercy.
If a poor person is detained, they must be released after five days.
The same applies to others; do not detain anyone.
If one fixes the mind on another person with long-term attachment, one will fail to guard oneself toward that person, and from this, evil will flow forth constantly.
As long as they have not yet dispersed, though bound, they remain at ease;
provided with ornaments, washing, food and drink, and appropriate medicines and fans.
Desiring that others become perfected vessels, the King establishes virtuous teachings out of compassion.
The virtuous and the wicked are all the same; it is not through anger or desire [that they differ].
Having reflected deeply and known this in truth, people increasingly give rise to rebellion.
Do not kill or oppress them; O King, I pray you, banish them to another land.
Regard yourself as an enemy; through the pure eye of a spiritual mentor, constantly maintain mindfulness without negligence, and vow to perform deeds in accordance with the Dharma.
Bestow abundant offerings upon those who have shown you kindness, so that they may receive their due reward.
As one contemplates the excellence or deficiency of virtue, so too shall be the retribution received.
Cultivating a welcoming demeanor is like a profusion of flowers; bestowing rewards and gifts is like the great fruit.
The king is the tree of patience whose shade is relied upon by his subjects, who are like birds gathering there for refuge.
A king who upholds the precepts and is able to practice generosity possesses majesty and wins the hearts of his subjects;
he is like a pellet of sugar candy, in which fragrance, texture, and flavor are blended together.
If a king relies upon the principles of the Dharma, then foolish ways will not prevail.
Without hardship or unrighteousness, there is constant joy in the Dharma.
It cannot be brought from past lives, nor can it be carried in;
the royal throne is obtained through the Dharma—do not destroy the Dharma for the sake of the throne.
The royal throne is like a shopkeeper’s stall; if it is handed down at whatever price is set, one should not seek to acquire it further. This is how you should conduct yourself.
The royal throne is like a shopkeeper’s stall; the transmission of the kingship is like the price set for it.
If one desires to further attain [liberation], this practice should be cultivated accordingly.
Even if a Wheel-Turning King gains the earth, or possesses the four continents, there is only the pleasure of body and mind; all other wealth and honor are empty.
It merely serves as an antidote to various sufferings; that which is called the bodily feeling of joy and pleasure, and mental pleasure, are all of the nature of conceptualization.
Having the antidote to suffering as its essence and conceptualization as its category, they are thus established.
All the pleasures of the world are empty and thus lack true reality.
Whether dwelling on an island, in a land, or in a settlement; whether it be seats, clothing, and the like;
food and drink, bedding, vehicles, wives, elephants, horses, or servants—[all are likewise empty].
If the mind follows a single object, it derives pleasure from that alone;
since other objects are not its conditions at that time, they are useless and void.
When the five sense organs take their five respective objects, if the mind does not engage in conceptual discrimination, [the senses remain as they are].
Although they may indeed constitute sense objects, pleasure does not arise from them.
These objects are what the sense faculties perceive; the others are neither subject nor object.
Therefore, as for the remaining faculties and objects, they truly lack any objective reality.
This object is what the sense-faculty perceives; the mind grasps its past aspect and, through discrimination, gives rise to a pure perception, thereby producing a pleasant feeling toward it.
A single atom is the object of the mind; the mind and the atom do not exist in the same temporal moment.
Since the mind is not separate from objects, and objects are likewise not separate from the mind;
just as you say that a son is born with parents as the cause, so too,
conditioned by the eye and forms, one says that consciousness and the rest arise.

The sense faculties and objects of the past and future do not exist, because they lack reality and do not emerge from these two time periods; thus, the present objects and faculties also lack reality.
It is like seeing a fire-wheel: this occurs because the sense faculty has become deranged.
Within present objects, the sense faculties and their engagement with objects are likewise so.
The five faculties and their spheres are of the nature of the four great elements;
because each great element is empty, it is not that objects and faculties do not exist.
If the four great elements were established as being separate from one another, then fire should burn even apart from fuel;
yet if they were not separate, they would have no distinct natures. The same judgment applies to the sense objects.
Since the two meanings of the four great elements are void, they cannot be established as a harmonious combination.
Since there is truly no harmony or identity, the object-field of form is not established.
Consciousness, feeling, perception, and formations—each and every one—is not established in essence;
they do not arise by combining through conditions, and because they do not exist, there is no combination.
Just as the conceptualization of joy and pleasure is established through the counteraction of suffering,
so too this conceived suffering is established through the destruction of pleasure.
Attachment to the union with pleasure ceases when it is conditioned by the signless (*animitta*).
One becomes free from craving for suffering; through this, non-arising is perceived.
If it is argued that, according to worldly convention, the mind is the seer, this is not so;
for apart from the seen, the seer cannot be established.
Observing the world through contemplative practice, one sees it as like an illusion, truly non-existent;
without grasping and without conceptual differentiation, parinirvāṇa is like a fire [that has gone out].
When a bodhisattva perceives in this way, they do not regress from awakening.
Drawn forth by great compassion, this continuity extends until Buddhahood.
The Buddha taught this path of cultivation for bodhisattvas within the Mahāyāna;
yet those people who lack wisdom and harbor hatred and jealousy bring harm upon themselves by repudiating it and refusing to accept it.
Failing to recognize merit and perceiving faults where there is virtue,
or out of hatred and envy for superior excellence, people thus slander the Mahāyāna.
If one knows that sin harms others, while merit is able to benefit them...
Therefore it is said: Those who slander do not recognize the malice they harbor toward virtue;
because they do not contemplate their own benefit but instead single-mindedly seek to benefit others, these vessels of the manifold virtues of the Mahāyāna reduce such slanderers to ashes.
Those who believe do so out of biased attachment; those who do not believe do so out of envy and hatred.
If even one who believes is burned by slander, how much more so one who is full of anger and jealousy?
To use poison to treat poison is as prescribed in medical treatises.
The same applies to the destruction of suffering and the eradication of evil; how could these statements be contradictory?
All phenomena are preceded by the mind and have the mind as their leader.

If suffering can bring benefit, one should accept it; how much more so pleasure?

A person of inferior status conceives of themselves as being no less than those who are their equals.

When an inferior person considers themselves equal to those who are superior,

Just as the various stages of the śrāvakas are taught within the Hīnayāna,

The first stage is named "Joyful," wherein joy is rare and marvelous because the three fetters are extinguished and one is born into the family of the Buddha.

Within hundreds of Buddha-worlds, he attains mastery without moving;
In Jambudvīpa and other continents, he becomes a great Wheel-Turning King,
Constantly turning the precious wheel and the wheel of Dharma throughout the world.
The second stage is named "The Stainless" (*vimalā*); In body, speech, and mind, all ten types of action are purified, And one attains mastery over their intrinsic nature.
Because of the retribution of this stage, One practices the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) before one's eyes.
Within the worlds of a thousand Buddhas, he attains mastery without wavering.
Like a seer or Śakra, Lord of Devas, he can eliminate the desires of the heavens;
neither celestial Māras nor external paths are able to move him.
The third is named Radiant Clarity; the light of tranquil wisdom arises therefrom.
Through meditative concentration and supernormal powers, desire, hatred, and delusion are extinguished.
Because of this, as the fruition of this stage, one manifests the practice of patience.
Within the worlds of ten thousand buddhas, he attains mastery without moving.
Acting as the sovereign of the Yāma Heaven, he extinguishes the habitual tendencies of the view of a self;
able to shatter all attachments of false teachers, he is capable of providing correct instruction.
The fourth is named Incineration; the flames of the fire of wisdom arise.
As the fruit of this stage, the perfection of vigor manifests.
By extensively cultivating the factors of enlightenment, one extinguishes delusions and gives rise to the Path.
The Lord of Tuṣita Heaven, having eliminated the views and precepts of non-Buddhists, attains mastery over rebirth;
